newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro takes in Rome sights before going home.
newsitem.headline: Castro takes in Rome sights before going home.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro toured Rome's ancient Forum on Wednesday and admired the Colosseum before departing for Havana, ending a high-profile visit which included an historic meeting with Pope John Paul.

Castro, who arrived in Italy on Saturday for a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit, spent his last hours in Rome taking in the sights, although he was surrounded by the tight security ring which has followed his every step during the stay.

The communist leader began his outing at the Michaelangelo- designed Capitoline square, where mayor Francesco Rutelli took him to see the gilded bronze statue of Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius seated on a horse which is housed there.
Rutelli recounted to reporters that he told Castro he had also shown the statue to U.S. President Bill Clinton in 1994 and that Clinton said he often read Aurelius's memoirs.
"I asked him whether he would ever make peace with Clinton," Rutelli said. "Castro replied, 'I don't know if he has the wisdom of Marcus Aurelius.'"
Instead of walking the short distance down the Capitoline Hill to the Forum, Castro was driven there accompanied by his large motorcade.
Castro got out and walked around for about 15 minutes, asking his guides about what he saw. Tourists gawked and restorers on scaffolding around one of the Forum's huge arches waved at him.
"I think it's a bit strange that he's taking this tour, but at least tourists get a chance to see him," said an Italian woman visiting Rome from the northern city of Trento.
Castro and his motorcade then drove slowly by the Colosseum.
"I don't have any opinion about his being a tourist, but politically I don't agree with him," said John Winkler, of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who was visiting the Colosseum with his family.
Castro had used his speech at the World Food Summit on Saturday to blast the 34-year-old U.S. embargo on Cuba and attack what he called the evils of capitalism.
The crowning moment of his visit was his meeting on Tuesday with the Pope, which he called "a miracle".

Castro told a news conference after the audience that the Pope had accepted an "unconditional" invitation to visit Cuba, probably sometime next year. "He will be received like a king and with respect".
The meeting, the first ever between Castro and the Pope, was seen as a major step forward in sometimes testy relations between the communist state and the Roman Catholic Church.
After his tourist jaunt on Wednesday, Castro went to Rome's Fiumicino Airport where his flight to Havana took off despite an air traffic controllers strike.
Airport officials said the plane got clearance because it was an official state flight.
